title: A Game of Pretend
mood: Selena copies smiles, mends radios and never cries. One night in a raid she finds out why she is different.

hero.alt: Selena, a blonde student with small red horns and a dark horned headband, smirks at the viewer with a round pink lollipop at her lips, blue shelves behind her.

segs.t: The last lamp in the workshop hung over the long bench.
Selena sorted salvage plates under it: whole ones for the night’s sale, cracked ones for the scrap bin. A fresh lollipop sat in her cheek.
The pull was still there in her cells, toward the bay, as it had all week. She sorted around it.
A plate slipped. Its edge opened her palm.
A bead of red came up. A thin purple seam drew the cut shut while she reached for the next plate.
She flexed the hand. Nothing hurt. Nobody had seen.
“You always walk away without a scratch,” a classmate had grumbled last week, picking glass out of his sleeve after a test rig blew.
Selena had always known she was different. The first cut she remembered had come from a window, in the rain.
Terrinia. The years after the storm.
Karina’s flat was two rooms at the top of a narrow stair. Her work boots stood by the door. The team radio sat on the shelf, and it was never off. All night it hissed street names and counts.
When the sirens went, Karina pulled the boots on.
“Door locked. If the sirens come close, you go down with her downstairs. I’m back when the last one’s carried out.”
After every strike she was gone all night, so Selena was alone a lot. She liked it.
Alone, she practiced smiles in the dark window glass. She tried the baker’s, and the one the woman downstairs wore for the landlord. She kept the ones that earned a second sweet.
One dawn Karina came in gray with ash and found her at the table, wearing a new one.
Karina stopped in the doorway. Then she laughed, tired, and dug out a second fruit drop.
“Where’d you get that one?”
“The baker.”
“It looks better on you.”
On wet mornings Karina held out a coat at the door.
“I’m not cold.”
“Coat anyway.”
She wore it because the other children did.
A boy in her class skinned his knee on the school steps and howled. For a week he picked at the scab. She watched it until it was gone. Her own scrapes were always gone before she thought to look.
Other children cried most days. Selena watched how they did it, in case she ever needed to.
When a storm came over the school, the children crawled under the tables. Selena stood at the window. Each crack of thunder made her bones go calm.
“Selena,” said the teacher. “Under the table.”
“Why?”
“Because everyone else is.”
So she went under the table, and lay there with her eyes open, listening.
Another day the teacher asked how to stop a fire running down a street.
“Knock down the next house first,” said Selena.
The class gasped. The teacher smiled. “That’s what the fire crews do. Clever girl.”
Neighbors brought her their dead radios. She had each one in pieces before the kettle boiled, and back together better than new.
“Talent, that one,” said the woman downstairs.
Destructive power and dangerous thoughts came naturally to her, yet the humans around her only praised them as signs of her unique talent. To her, it was all a game of pretend.
Selena smiled, and reached for the next radio.
She had outgrown two pairs of boots when the raid came.
It came at night, in rain, with Karina on shift. The whole block went down the stairs in their nightclothes, in a line toward the shelter. The woman from downstairs had Selena by the hand.
Something hit two streets over. The line broke. People ran every way at once, and the woman’s hand let go.
Then she was alone in a side street, in the rain. Far off, a siren rose and fell.
An Ender came around the corner.
It was tall and gray, taller than the doorways. Violet light burned in the seams of its shell. The stones cracked under its feet.
She did not run.
Its shoulder caught a window as it came, and the glass burst over her.
Its head turned. The violet light found her.
Then the hum came, deep in her bones. It was the hum of the first night, the one that had felt like home.
The Ender looked at her for one breath. Then its head turned away. It walked on past her, so close that rain off its shell spattered her face.
Her arm stung.
She looked down. A shard of the window had opened her bare forearm. Red ran with the rain to her wrist.
Under the red, something moved.
Purple. It came up out of the cut in fine threads and drew the edges together, the way Karina’s needle drew a torn pocket shut. The rain washed the red away. The skin lay whole.
She held the arm out in the rain and turned it over. Then over again.
That isn’t what blood does,
she thought.
I watched his knee for a week.
The street was empty. Nobody had seen.
She stood there until the siren stopped. Then she walked to the shelter by herself.
At dawn Karina found her there. She knelt and looked her over, the way she looked over everyone she carried out. Arms, hands, face.
“Any cuts?”
Selena held out both arms. They were clean.
“No,” she said.
Karina let out a breath. Her shoulders came down. She pressed her forehead to the girl’s wet hair and stayed there.
When Karina drew back, Selena watched her face. So that was how relief went. She kept it with the smiles.
“Home,” said Karina.
It looked right at me,
she thought, for days.
Why did it walk on?
Then she went to the city library.
She knew the word Ender. Every child in Terrinia did. She had never thought it could mean her.
On the wall inside the door hung a notice from the Shield of Dawnbreak: what to do in a raid.
Enders are living machines. A gray metal shell. Under it, living purple tissue. Do not hide behind a downed Ender. They do not attack each other, and they will walk around their own to reach you.
She read it twice. Then only the last line.
The head turning away. The threads in the cut.
Something in her clicked, like a part seating home in a radio.
So that’s the rule,
she thought.
They don’t hit their own. It didn’t hit me.
Around her, people turned pages at the long tables. A girl her size read aloud to her mother. Nobody looked up.
I always knew I wasn’t one of them,
she thought.
Now I know what I am. So nobody else gets to know.
Her thumb found the place on her forearm. It was as smooth as the rest.
Karina digs people out of what Enders break.
She asked me about cuts. I said no.
Not even Karina.
At the long table the girl turned a page, and her mother laughed. Selena stood by the notice until the story ended.
She walked home past the bakery and gave the baker his own smile. He waved.
At the flat she set her boots beside Karina’s. The radio hissed street names. Karina slept through it, still in her coat.
By the time her boots pinched again, she had found the roof.
Karina’s building had a flat roof and a water tank. In storms Selena climbed up, where the rain was loud enough to hide anything.
There she tested it. She let the purple come up along her arms, then called it back down. It obeyed her every time. The lightning hid its glow.
One night she let it run further than ever, up to her shoulders. Thunder broke right over the tank. Selena spread her arms in the rain and grinned at the sky.
“Ahh, I’m getting a dangerous vibe. Right now, I might be super dangerous.”
Two small hard points pushed up through her hair. She touched them. Horns, no bigger than her thumb tips.
She drew them back in, and her hair lay flat again. She kept them in after that.
When she came down, soaked, Karina looked up from the table.
“Not in the lightning.”
“Fine.”
Karina threw her a towel and pushed a cup of tea across.

Their fingers touched on the cup. Selena’s hands were warm. They were always warm after a storm, when other children came in from the rain blue-lipped and shaking. All that winter she had not been ill once.
Karina’s fingers stayed on hers a breath longer than usual. Then she let go, and picked up her needle again.
Older again, Selena found the fence.
Most evenings at dusk she walked to the research base and stood at its outer fence. Something on the benches in there hummed, low, almost like her own bones.
One evening a small girl crossed the yard with an armful of parts. She wore a child-sized lab coat. A white robot rabbit floated at her shoulder.
The girl saw her through the fence. She shifted the parts to one arm and waved.
Selena did not wave back.
In the workshop, the plate still lay by the lamp, its edge red.
Selena wiped it with a rag and dropped it on the pile for the night’s sale. Then she turned her palm up under the light. It was clean.
